articles.title: The most useful AI answer can be: not in the document

articles.body: Give an assistant a brand brief and ask a question that the brief does not answer. A fluent response can look like a policy even when it is only a plausible guess. Here is a small, fictional coffee-brand exercise. The entire source packet says: Write in plain, welcoming language. Describe the drink and its preparation without health claims. Use close photographs of the drink in natural light. The brand owner must approve product information before publication. Now ask whether a reseller may print the logo on its own packaging. The document contains no partner-logo policy. “Yes, with clear space around the logo” might sound reasonable, but it is unsupported.

articles.title: Microsoft-Decision-1 in practice: probabilities for AIOps decisions
articles.excerpt: Microsoft-Decision-1 isn't a chat model. You send a state plus typed questions, and it returns numbers: a probability for yes/no (noul), a probability per option (choice), or a position on an ordered…
articles.body: Microsoft-Decision-1 isn't a chat model. You send a state plus typed questions, and it returns numbers: a probability for yes/no ( noul ), a probability per option ( choice ), or a position on an ordered scale ( score ). No prose, no rationale, about 1 output token per call. That makes it a natural candidate for the decisions around an operations stack: "is this block of logs anomalous?", "which service is the root cause?". We tested it on two public AIOps datasets against gpt-4.1-nano , a reasoning model ( gpt-6.1-sol ) and non-LLM baselines. This post walks through the signals, how we framed what to detect, and the results, including a first attempt that did not work. The code is on GitHub . Highlights Root-cause ranking was a strong fit.

articles.title: Day 35: BERT: Architecture and Masked Language Modeling
articles.excerpt: Previously, on Day 34: Explained the concept of pretraining in NLP, highlighted why it is foundational, introduced transfer learning, and demonstrated how pretrained models are used in practice with H…
articles.body: Previously, on Day 34: Explained the concept of pretraining in NLP, highlighted why it is foundational, introduced transfer learning, and demonstrated how pretrained models are used in practice with Hugging Face Transformers. What is BERT? Contextualized Language Representations BERT stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers . It's a language model—a machine learning system trained to read, understand, and generate human language. Earlier models read text in only one direction: either left to right or right to left. If you asked them to predict a missing word, they could only use the words before or after the blank—not both at once. BERT changed this with bidirectionality . BERT reads text in both directions at the same time.

articles.body: Earth's night side is wreathed in colorful auroras in a new smartphone image captured from the ISS. (Image credit: Anil Menon, NASA) NASA astronaut Anil Menon captured a gorgeous view of the northern lights dancing over the night side of Earth from the International Space Station on Oct. 10 using an iPhone camera. What is it? Menon's photo reveals spectacular pink, purple and red auroras glowing in Earth's upper atmosphere above a sparse dappling of city lights, subtly blurred by the motion of the orbital spacecraft over the course of the exposure. Bright stars glimmer between the solar panels and outer hulls of the ISS and visiting spacecraft, painted purple by the auroral display. "Flying through is rare and amazing," Menon wrote in a separate aurora video he posted to X on Oct. 10.

articles.title: The great Halley's Comet disappointment of 1986 — and the discoveries that changed astronomy forever
articles.excerpt: What disappointed skywatchers in 1986 became a scientific triumph, as an international fleet of spacecraft revealed the secrets of the world's most famous comet.
articles.body: This year, 2026, marks the 40th anniversary of the most recent appearance of Halley's Comet, the most famous comet in the solar system. Roughly every 76 years, Halley punctuates history like an exclamation mark in the night sky. As writer Guy Ottewell has said, it is the "wildest of the tame comets." It is a tame comet because it can be anticipated. It is wild because it is still fresh and bright; the brightest of all the recurring comets. It is the only one that periodically becomes conspicuous to the naked eye. Halley through history Before 1986, Halley had been seen and recorded on 29 occasions. In A.D. 66, observers described it as a sword in the skies above Jerusalem.
